extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly / educated general public interested in science and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Short, illustrated notes and reports for a popular-science magazine: concise accounts of experiments, natural-history observations, scientific theories, public-health arguments, and expedition narratives aimed at a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational-health measures for elevator workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Rochester considers a regulation and limitation of the hours of continuous labor, the sanitary regulation of lodging and boarding houses, and restriction in the use of ardent spirits, essential parts of any measures for checking elevator pneumonia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive standard for preventing 'elevator pneumonia': limit continuous work hours, improve sanitary conditions of housing and boarding, and restrict alcohol use. Presented as core policy interventions to reduce occupational pulmonary disease among shovellers working in dust-laden, close atmospheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration of causation (green color of oysters)
rubrics_metrics.description: M. Puysegur's experiments: green slime (navicula) scraped and placed with perfectly white, previously-washed oysters; control oysters put into ordinary sea-water; in twenty-six hours oysters exposed to diatoms acquired a marked greenish hue while controls remained unaltered; experiment repeated several times; greenness disappeared after a few days in ordinary sea-water and reappeared when put in fresh water containing the navicula; diatom carapaces were found strewn through the digestive tubes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence-standard illustrated: use of cleaned controls, repetition of the trial, observation of a dose-response relation (more green with more diatoms), demonstration of reversibility, and direct anatomical observation (diatom carapaces in digestive tracts) — multiple converging lines of evidence to support a causal claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for successful deep-sea exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: The French commission 'accomplished an exploration' of the Gulf of Gascony and a submarine valley, having collected at least five hundred species, nearly all new to the fauna of the Gulf, and some new to science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures of success for exploratory natural-history expeditions include quantity of specimens collected, novelty (species new to the region or to science), thoroughness of sampling, and documentation by qualified naturalists — outcomes emphasized as indicators of a 'completely successful' expedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for judging synthetic mineral production
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition necessary to be fulfilled in this manufacture is that of obtaining crystalline products as nearly as possible identical in composition and appearance with the minerals to be reproduced; workers sometimes accept microscopic crystals as sufficient; various processes (fusion, solvents, vapor deposition, reactions, electrical excitement, temperature variation) are used to obtain specific minerals and mineral associations that resemble natural rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity criteria for artificial mineral synthesis: reproduce crystalline habit, composition, and associations (appearance close to natural minerals); use appropriate methods (mimicking natural conditions or independent techniques); acceptability can range from microscopic crystals to macroscopic material depending on purpose; reproducibility and close resemblance to natural specimens are decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific-theory evaluation: predictive power and empirical basis
rubrics_metrics.description: M. Delaunay's earthquake theory is presented in terms of producing predictions of seismic 'periods' (dates when earthquakes may be looked for) by positing planetary passages through meteor groups; M. Faye criticizes Laplace's nebular hypothesis for invoking 'an immense degree of heat' without evidence and proposes instead an explanation based on observed nebulae that would develop heat naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standards for good scientific theorizing: theories should be grounded in observable evidence, avoid arbitrary or unsupported assumptions, and ideally yield testable predictions (temporal forecasts, explanatory mechanisms). The text contrasts theories judged by their empirical plausibility and predictive scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health policy evaluation: quarantine versus sanitary inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lancet denies value in ordinary quarantine practice — contraband and late imposition often defeat it; quarantine has diverted attention from true prevention. England and Denmark ceased to rely upon quarantine, adopting medical inspection and sanitary administration so that districts can deal with infectious disease effectively; port sanitary authorities can inspect arrivals, isolate sick persons, and disinfect — doing what efficient quarantine aims to do but more effectively and with less hardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-evaluation criteria: prioritize measures that are practically efficient, timely, enforceable, proportionate in cost, and that minimize hardships and commerce disruption. Medical inspection and decentralized sanitary administration are recommended as superior to broad quarantine when they can isolate cases and apply disinfection without excessive social/economic cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and cautions for statistical study of social phenomena (suicide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Morselli's compilation shows increasing suicides across many European countries; he notes that part of the increase may be due to better reporting and that official reports 'must be accepted with reserve.' He arranges predispositions under cosmic/natural, ethnic, social, and individual headings and reports patterns (city>country, men>women, increase with age, marriage preventive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological standards: use official statistics but adjust for reporting improvements and biases; classify and examine multiple classes of influence (environmental, ethnic, social, individual); analyze demographic correlates (sex, age, marital status, urbanization); exercise caution about inferring motives from limited official reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-factor demographic analysis of fertility trends
rubrics_metrics.description: M. A. Legoyt assigns France's slow population growth to moral, political, economical, and physiological causes: decay of religious beliefs enabling voluntary limitation of fertility; increased illegitimacy, abortions, still-births and infanticides; economic prudence among the relatively comfortable; urbanization; rising costs of living; division of paternal estates encouraging fewer children; war losses; later ages at marriage; female employment as nurses removing childbearing periods; long military service delaying marriage; complex/expensive marriage procedures; alcoholism affecting reproductive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards for demographic explanation: consider a broad set of interrelated causal factors (cultural/religious norms, economic incentives and constraints, demographic behaviors like marriage age and urban migration, public policies such as conscription, and health/lifestyle factors). Use comparative regional/time-series data to separate effects (e.g., fertility by department, changes over decades).
